questions: Did this walking difficulty begin suddenly?
Do you have weakness or numbness on one side of your body?
Do you experience spinning dizziness or loss of balance when sitting still?
Does your walking improve when you are distracted or when walking backward?
Have you recently had a significant emotional stressor or traumatic event?
Do you fall despite being able to move your legs normally while lying in bed?
Do you have stiffness or slowness of movement in your arms or legs?
Does either foot drag or catch on the floor when you walk?
Do you have pain in your back, hips, knees, or legs that limits walking?
Do you have urinary or bowel-control problems?
Have you had a stroke, spinal-cord injury, or other neurological illness?
Do you use a walking aid outside the hospital?
Has the eye-movement problem progressed gradually over weeks or months?
Do you have double vision or drooping eyelids?
Do you have difficulty swallowing or speaking?
Do you have involuntary jerking movements, tremor, or muscle twitching?
Do you have reduced hearing or difficulty seeing in dim light?
Have you had episodes of confusion, excessive daytime sleepiness, or abnormal movements during sleep?
Did the eye-movement abnormality and unsteady gait develop over a few days to two weeks?
Did you have a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection in the month before these symptoms began?
Have you recently received a vaccination?
Have you had dry mouth, blurred vision, fixed or enlarged pupils, constipation, or difficulty urinating?
Have you eaten home-canned food or food preserved in an unusual way shortly before becoming unwell?
Have you had facial weakness, limb weakness, or trouble breathing?
Did these eye-movement and gait problems begin in childhood or adolescence?
Do close relatives have similar eye-movement problems, gait difficulty, or unexplained neurological disease?
Do your symptoms worsen with sustained activity and improve after rest?
Have you had thyroid disease, diabetes, or another autoimmune disorder?
Have you taken medications known to affect eye movements, such as sedatives, antipsychotics, anti-seizure drugs, or amiodarone?
Have you had episodes of headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, or seizures?
Are your pupils normal in size and reactive to light?
Is the eye-movement limitation present even when your head is moved to trigger the vestibulo-ocular reflex?
Have you had weight loss, diarrhea, abdominal pain, joint pains, fever, or enlarged lymph nodes?
Have you had chronic cough, loss of smell, or a persistent imbalance in the dark?
Do you have a history of heavy alcohol use, poor nutrition, or bariatric surgery?
Are you older than 50 years?
orders: Perform a complete bedside neurological examination, including assessment for resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia with finger tapping and hand opening/closing, postural stability, arm swing, turning, and initiation/freezing of gait.
Perform the pull test for postural instability.
Obtain a brain MRI without contrast.
Perform a slit-lamp examination for Kayser–Fleischer corneal rings.
Measure serum ceruloplasmin and serum copper, and obtain a 24-hour urinary copper excretion.
Test for Niemann–Pick disease type C using plasma oxysterols and NPC1/NPC2 genetic testing.
Perform formal vestibular-ocular reflex and saccadic eye-movement testing, including video-oculography.
Obtain plasma oxysterols and lysosphingomyelin-508, followed by NPC1/NPC2 gene sequencing if abnormal or if clinical suspicion remains high.
Obtain cerebrospinal fluid analysis, including cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, and infectious PCR testing for Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei).
Perform plasma oxysterol and lysosphingomyelin-509 testing, followed by NPC1/NPC2 sequencing and filipin staining of cultured skin fibroblasts if screening is nondiagnostic.
Perform a mitochondrial disease panel including POLG, TWNK, OPA1, and mitochondrial DNA, with serum lactate and creatine kinase.
served: deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
